articles.title: In a Pennsylvania town, 194 families have assembled 4,466 acres for a potential $1.4 billion data-centre deal; officials approved new zoning, but the land sale and proposed $12 million hospital are not final
articles.summary: Local officials in a rural Pennsylvania community have approved new zoning rules, bringing 194 local families one step closer to a possible $1.4 billion
articles.body: Local officials in a rural Pennsylvania community have approved new zoning rules, bringing 194 local families one step closer to a possible $1.4 billion land deal for a large technology and energy campus. The Salem Township Board of Supervisors voted 2-0 on 27 October 2026 to expand the area's Special Data Center Overlay district, according to GlobeNewswire. The decision covers 4,466 acres of farmland, homes, and former agricultural properties in Luzerne County. The land has been selected for the proposed Salem 3 Campus. Despite this important approval, the multi-billion-dollar deal is not yet final. It still depends on completed property contracts, power agreements, and other required project approvals. A proposed $12 million micro-hospital, which is part of a community benefits package, also depends on final agreements.High-capacity energy hub attracts tech developersThe project plans to build a 4-gigawatt digital infrastructure and energy campus by using the large amount of electricity already generated in the township. Salem Township is part of the PJM Interconnection wholesale electricity market. It is also home to the Susquehanna nuclear power plant and a major combined-cycle natural gas power facility. Jack Sordoni, co-founder of development company 4-3 Glennbrook Group, spoke about why the location was suitable after the public hearing. "Data centers are not a yes or no question. It's about where and how," Sordoni stated, according to GlobeNewswire. "In this case, 'where' happens to be between two nuclear towers, a massive gas plant, major electrical infrastructure and virtually unlimited fuel sources. The 'how' comes from embracing the landowners, their value and their dignity, and coming together as a community to recognize the opportunity a project like this promises." Documents submitted by the developers show that the proposed campus will use closed-loop cooling systems. These systems are designed to prevent the project from taking large amounts of water from local sources. The plans also aim to meet state electricity grid requirements set out in Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro's Executive Order 2026-05.Landowners seek economic return after previous successful saleThe decision by 194 local households to work together represents one of the largest coordinated private land deals in Northeastern Pennsylvania's history. The plan follows an earlier land deal in the same township. According to 4-3 Glennbrook Group, the development company previously brought together landowners for the neighboring Salem 2 project. That process resulted in a $586 million sale to data center operator QTS. Dave Scoblick, co-founder and principal at 4-3 Glennbrook Group, explained that a significant amount of work remains before the land sale can be completed. "We're grateful to the Board of Supervisors for the time and care they put into this decision, and to everyone who came out and spoke, whether they were for it or had questions," Scoblick said in statements released through GlobeNewswire. "Tonight's vote is a big step for 194 Salem Township families, but we're still not at the finish line. We have a lot of work ahead, and we're going to keep doing it transparently alongside the township and our neighbors."Community benefit package includes healthcare facilityThe project plan includes a proposed $43 million Community Benefit Agreement. The money would support local government services and improvements to regional infrastructure. One of the main parts of the proposal is $12 million for a new local micro-hospital. The facility would bring urgent and emergency medical services back to the area. Residents lost their main local medical centre after Berwick Hospital closed permanently. The project also plans to keep around 75 per cent of the 4,466-acre site as natural buffer areas, open spaces, and protected environmental zones. Participating landowners have also suggested using part of the money from the land sale to support Heritage Park. The planned year-round recreational space would be located on the former Beach Haven Carnival grounds.Mike Cabell, principal at 4-3 Glennbrook Group, spoke about how the families considered future generations when making their decisions. "These families made a big decision about their land, and they made it with their kids and grandkids in mind," Cabell stated to GlobeNewswire. "Tonight's vote shows that decision was worth it. They stuck with this through every meeting and every question, and we're going to get this done for them in a way that benefits the community for generations." According to reporting by GovTech, communities across Pennsylvania continue to discuss the effects of large data center projects. Local concerns include industrial development, growing electricity demand, and the tax benefits these projects could bring. These discussions are becoming more important as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure increases across the country. The Salem 3 project will now move forward to further technical reviews, environmental studies, and assessments of its connection to the electricity grid. These steps must be completed before the property transfers can officially close.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Los Angeles tenant paid a $19,500 deposit on a $9,750-a-month rental home, but landlords kept it after he left; an appeals court upheld a $61,801.67 judgment and struck down a $1,000 cap on court costs
articles.summary: A Los Angeles tenant who paid a $19,500 deposit to rent a $9,750-a-month home has won a major legal victory against the property’s landlords. In Aviles v.
articles.body: A Los Angeles tenant who paid a $19,500 deposit to rent a $9,750-a-month home has won a major legal victory against the property’s landlords. In Aviles v. Shenon, the California Court of Appeal upheld a $61,801.67 judgment in favour of former tenant Eric Aviles, rejecting the landlords’ attempt to limit court costs to $1,000 under a clause in the lease, as per Justia U.S. Law. The decision confirms that a landlord cannot use a private lease provision to override a tenant’s statutory right to recover litigation costs after prevailing in court.The case began when Aviles rented a home in Los Angeles for $9,750 a month and paid a deposit of $19,500. After he left the property, the landlords, including defendants identified in the appeal as Shenon and others, retained the entire deposit. Aviles sued to recover it, and the litigation eventually produced a judgment that included the deposit, damages, attorney fees and costs. Read more details about this particular case, as per Justia U.S. Law, here:What the tenant claimedAviles argued that the landlords had no legal basis to keep his deposit after he vacated the home. Under California law, residential landlords must follow specific procedures when withholding all or part of a security deposit, including providing an itemised statement of deductions and returning any amount not properly retained.The trial court ruled for Aviles and entered a judgment of $61,801.67. This amount included not only damages related to return of the deposit dispute, but also reasonable attorney fees and costs permitted under the applicable statutes. The landlords appealed the judgment both on its merits and as to the amount of costs awarded.The appeal was over a narrow but important issue: could the landlords rely on a lease clause limiting recoverable court costs to $1,000? They argued that the clause should limit Aviles’s recovery even though he had prevailed in the case.The $1,000 cost capThe lease contained a provision limiting court costs to $1,000. The landlords argued that this provision should control the amount Aviles could recover as costs after winning his case. In effect, they claimed the contract had set a ceiling on the litigation expenses a tenant could pass on to them.The Court of Appeal rejected that argument. It held that the lease’s $1,000 cap could not override the statutory cost award available to a prevailing tenant. The court ruled that a private agreement cannot take away a tenant's statutory rights, especially when the law is intended to protect tenants and to give them meaningful access to the courts.The conclusion is of practical importance. Landlords could set a low cap on recoverable costs, which might discourage tenants from bringing legitimate claims because the costs of litigation might exceed the money involved. By striking down the cap, the appellate court reinforced the principle that tenant-protective statutes take precedence over conflicting lease terms.Why the judgment stoodThe appellate court affirmed the $61,801.67 judgment in Aviles’s favour. The decision means the landlords cannot use the lease’s cost limitation to reduce the financial consequences of losing the case.The ruling also underscores that a security deposit is not simply money a landlord may keep after a tenant moves out. California law treats deposits as the tenant’s money unless the landlord can justify specific deductions, such as unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, or cleaning costs permitted by statute. A landlord who fails to follow the required process risks liability for improper withholding.In this case, the landlords’ decision to retain the full $19,500 deposit became the foundation of a much larger judgment. Once attorney fees and statutory costs were added, the financial outcome grew well beyond the original deposit amount.What the case means for tenantsFor tenants, the decision is a reminder that lease language does not always mean what it appears to say. A clause limiting court costs may look enforceable, but it cannot lawfully eliminate a statutory right to recover costs after winning a landlord-tenant dispute.The case also illustrates why documentation matters. Tenants should maintain records of the lease, payment records, move in and move out photographs, repair requests and any written communication with the landlord. These materials can help establish the condition of the property and whether a deposit deduction is justified.Most significantly, the decision suggests that California courts can enforce tenant protections even when a lease attempts to contract around them. A tenant who prevails in a deposit case may be able to recover not only the wrongfully withheld money, but also fees and costs that make litigation financially viable.What landlords should knowIt’s a warning shot across the bows of landlords to the dangers of holding a deposit without good legal cause. A landlord must be able to document why money was withheld and comply with California’s notice and accounting requirements.The decision also cautions landlords against relying on lease clauses that conflict with statutory tenant rights. Even if both parties signed the agreement, a provision that limits a tenant’s statutory cost recovery may be unenforceable. In this case, the $1,000 cap did not protect the landlords from the full cost award.The broader lesson is that security-deposit disputes can become expensive when handled improperly. What began as a $19,500 deposit dispute ended with a judgment of $61,801.67, demonstrating that legal fees and costs can quickly exceed the amount originally contested.A clear message from the courtThe California Court of Appeal’s decision in Aviles v. Shenon does more than resolve one deposit dispute. It affirms that tenants who win valid claims can recover statutory costs, even where a lease tries to cap those costs at a nominal amount.For Aviles, the ruling preserves a $61,801.67 judgment after the landlords kept his $19,500 deposit. For renters across California, it reinforces a simple principle: a lease cannot take away rights the law gives tenants, and a landlord who wrongfully withholds a deposit may end up paying far more than the money it kept.You use AI every day. articles.title: Scottish charity manager Lindsay MacCallum stole more than £95,000 from two cancer charities, including one set up in memory of her best friend's daughter; she was jailed for three years
articles.summary: For years, Lindsay MacCallum held positions that gave her access to money raised for people affected by cancer.
articles.body: For years, Lindsay MacCallum held positions that gave her access to money raised for people affected by cancer. She worked with two charitable organisations in Scotland, handling fundraising and financial arrangements, while donations were intended to support their respective causes. But an investigation into missing funds eventually uncovered unauthorised payments, forged signatures and money transferred into accounts belonging to her and members of her family. The amounts involved exceeded £95,000, taken over a period spanning roughly a decade. MacCallum, a former charity manager from Aberfoyle in Stirlingshire, was eventually brought before Falkirk Sheriff Court, where she admitted her involvement in the fraudulent activity and received a three-year prison sentence.How Lindsay MacCallum misused her position at Anthony Nolan charityMacCallum, 61, had a longstanding association with the charity sector before the offences came to light. Between 1995 and 2012, she worked as a fundraising manager for the Anthony Nolan charity, an organisation involved in leukaemia treatment and stem cell donation. Her responsibilities included handling financial transactions, although payments by cheque required approval from one of two authorised office-bearers.The local fundraising group, Aberfoyle Friends of Anthony Nolan Trust, continued operating its bank account even after both authorised signatories had left the organisation in 2007. MacCallum had been made redundant from her position with Anthony Nolan in 2012, but the account remained accessible to her.The court heard that she continued withdrawing money by using signatures that did not belong to the former office-bearers. Between July 2011 and September 2016, eight cheques were issued without proper authorisation. Together, they amounted to £9,505.Both former signatories later told police that they had not signed the documents. They also identified the handwriting on the cheques as MacCallum's, helping establish how the payments had been made.How a friendship led to a £85,978 cancer charity fraudThe larger part of the fraud involved Friends of Rainbow Valley, a charity established in July 2012 by a woman who had previously been MacCallum's close friend. The organisation was created in memory of the friend's daughter and employed MacCallum as a paid project development manager.Their professional relationship continued for several years, with MacCallum entrusted with responsibilities connected to the charity's work and finances. However, the friendship eventually deteriorated. She remained involved with the organisation until March 2022, when she stepped down from her position.The financial discrepancies were discovered several months later. In August 2022, charity officials examined the accounts and found transactions that could not be properly explained, including payments associated with the organisation's annual fundraising ball.The review raised questions about where the money had gone. When confronted about the missing funds, MacCallum admitted that she had taken money from the charity. She also acknowledged her actions publicly in a Facebook post, writing: "I've let everybody down. I'm so sorry."As reported by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, the investigation established that £85,978.48 had been fraudulently obtained from Friends of Rainbow Valley. Combined with the £9,505 taken from the Anthony Nolan fundraising account, the total came to £95,483.48.How the stolen charity money was distributedDetails presented in court showed that the money did not simply disappear through a single transaction. Between 2013 and 2021, MacCallum paid substantial sums into several bank accounts connected to her family.Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported that two personal accounts held by MacCallum received a combined £48,027. A further £5,045 went into a joint bank account she shared with her husband, while £1,670 was deposited into accounts belonging to her adult children.Other spending was traced through her credit card and retail purchases. The court heard that £21,056 had been spent on a credit card, while another £4,210 went towards purchases from Next.Three-year prison sentence and proceeds of crime actionMacCallum appeared at Falkirk Sheriff Court after admitting two charges relating to a fraudulent scheme carried out between 2011 and 2021. The court sentenced her to three years in prison.The case also prompted action to recover the money obtained through the offences. MacCallum is to face confiscation proceedings under proceeds of crime legislation, which allows authorities to pursue the recovery of financial gains from criminal activity.Helen Nisbet, Procurator Fiscal for Tayside, Central and Fife, addressed the breach of responsibility involved in the case. She said MacCallum had been entrusted with financial oversight of money raised by two cancer charities, but had used that access to take donations intended for people affected by the disease. Nisbet also stressed the importance of maintaining public confidence in charitable organisations, particularly when people contribute money believing it will reach those who need support.

articles.title: Florida-based cruise ship company promised never-ending voyage, took tens of thousands of dollars from passengers, then abandoned them in Cambodia citing fuel costs
articles.summary: A cruise ship that offered passengers the opportunity to live on board for years has left Cambodia without its residents after its owner suspended
articles.body: A cruise ship that offered passengers the opportunity to live on board for years has left Cambodia without its residents after its owner suspended operations, citing soaring fuel costs linked to the Iran war.The Villa Vie Odyssey departed from the port town of Sihanoukville early on Wednesday (November 4), carrying around 50 crew members but no passengers. More than 200 people who had paid tens of thousands of dollars for long-term stays on the vessel were forced to disembark last week.The ship's Florida-based owner, Villa Vie Residences, suspended operations, saying rising fuel prices caused by the Iran war had made running the vessel prohibitively expensive.According to Taing Sochitkrishna, head of the Sihanoukville tourism department, in Cambodia, around 100 passengers remained in Cambodia, while the others largely flew to other destinations in the region.Passengers collected their remaining belongings from the ship on Tuesday, with many saying they did not expect to return."There are still many things on the ship that I wish I could take with me," Shirine Thomas, from Wilmington, North Carolina, said after collecting some of her belongings.Rent a ship, live permanently on the seaThe Villa Vie Odyssey had been sailing around the world for at least 755 days. It was among a handful of cruise ships offering passengers the option of renting or purchasing long-term, and even permanent, residences on board.However, the sudden suspension of operations has left passengers uncertain about the future of their expensive arrangements.Mary Ann Demsar, a 67-year-old retired high school teacher from Ontario, Canada, said passengers had received little information from the company about what would happen next. "We don't get any clear indication from the owners of Villa Vie as to what is happening," she said."They've been so quiet, the only information we get is from the wonderful government and the representatives here in Cambodia."Where is the cruise ship headed?The ship's final destination remained unclear after it departed Cambodia. Some passengers and maritime tracking websites indicated that it was heading towards Singapore. The ship left behind passengers who had invested tens of thousands of dollars in the promise of living aboard a cruise ship while travelling around the world.CBS News reported that once the ship gets to Singapore, it could potentially be auctioned off. But Villa Vie's CEO Mikael "Mike" Petterson said they're exploring all their options to get the vessel back.57-year-old sold his condo to pay for cruiseJoel Greiff, 57, decided to sell his condo in Naples, Florida, and take an early withdrawal from his 401(k) to pay for permanent residency via one of Villa Vie's Endless Horizons programs. New York Times reported that Greiff paid $350,000 for a long-term stay. He boarded the ship on Oct. 1 but was told he would have to vacate the vessel after just 26 days.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Iowa family spent decades using 3.53 acres beside Owl Lake Creek as a childhood playground; after a dream discussed for 10 to 15 years, they donated the land and it has now been dedicated as a public park
articles.summary: A piece of land that once held decades of childhood memories for an Iowa family has found a new purpose, becoming a public space where future generations
articles.body: A piece of land that once held decades of childhood memories for an Iowa family has found a new purpose, becoming a public space where future generations can enjoy nature. The 3.53-acre property, located beside Owl Lake Creek in Lakeside, has been dedicated as Massop Legacy Park following a donation by John and Marlene Massop to Buena Vista County. According to a November 2 report by Storm Lake Radio, also carried by Iowa Media Wire, the dedication brought together members of the Massop family, county officials and local residents to mark the addition to the county's conservation system. The land lies just south of the Storm Lake Outlet Dam, close to Bel Air Access, where Owl Lake Creek flows out of Storm Lake. What was once part of the Massop family's personal landscape will now be preserved as a natural area accessible to the wider community.The idea behind the donation had been taking shape for years. Doug Massop had discussed the possibility of turning the property into a public park with his late father, John, around 10 to 15 years ago. His parents had farmed the land, and the family recognised that its location near the creek and lake outlet offered an opportunity to create something that could benefit the community long after their own time there.Over the past four to five years, Doug continued working towards making that vision a reality. He approached city, county and state officials, as well as the Iowa Department of Natural Resources, to explore how the property could be transferred and developed for public use. Buena Vista County Conservation Director Greg Johnson played an important role in bringing the different stakeholders together and helping move the donation forward.A natural space with room to growRather than immediately transforming the property into a developed recreational destination, the county plans to focus on protecting and improving its existing natural environment. The 3.53 acres contain a combination of wooded sections, grassland and the creek, creating different habitats for local wildlife. Conservation efforts will initially centre on encouraging native prairie vegetation, managing invasive plant species and maintaining water quality along Owl Lake Creek.Some early improvements are already in place. Local Boy Scouts have built nesting boxes for the property, while other habitat features have also been donated. The county is considering opening sections of the existing fence line and creating walking paths that will allow visitors to explore parts of the land.These initial changes are expected to be managed largely through the conservation department's existing staff and resources. Larger recreational projects, however, remain at an early stage, with no dedicated funding or final development plans currently in place.A longer-term vision for the areaThe family hopes the park could eventually become part of a larger recreational network around Storm Lake. One possibility is a bike trail that would connect different parts of the area and offer residents more opportunities to enjoy the outdoors. The donation agreement also leaves room for additional infrastructure in the future. If a nearby housing development moves ahead, the possibility of constructing a bridge across the creek and extending walking paths could be explored.For now, the priority remains keeping the property accessible while allowing its natural features to thrive. The intention is to ensure that the land remains a place where wildlife can find suitable habitat and residents can spend time outdoors without extensive development changing its character. Massop Legacy Park also adds to Buena Vista County Conservation's existing network of public spaces. The department manages 17 areas covering more than 1,200 acres, including parks, wildlife refuges, historic sites and other natural areas.For the Massop family, the dedication marks the completion of an idea that began with conversations between a father and son more than a decade ago. What was once a familiar stretch of land associated with family life and childhood memories will now have a different kind of legacy, offering the wider community a place to connect with nature for years to come.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Utah girl missing for 17 months was rescued from an Oregon home after she contacted another child online; federal agents monitored a video call, and a 39-year-old man now faces a criminal charge
articles.summary: A 17-year-old girl missing from Utah for 17 months has been rescued from an Oregon home after contacting another child online. A 39-year-old man faces federal charges for transporting her across state lines for illegal sexual activity.
articles.body: A 17-year-old girl who disappeared from Utah in May last year was found at an Oregon home after an online conversation with another minor helped authorities establish her whereabouts. Investigators arranged a video call with the girl while FBI agents monitored the conversation, leading to a rescue operation and the arrest of a 39-year-old man.The girl was located on Sunday at a residence in Huntington, Oregon, after investigators received a tip about her possible location. Adam Hunter Harmel was arrested during a traffic stop in Ontario, about 30 miles from the home, according to the AP.Harmel has been charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. The federal complaint was filed on November 2 in the US District Court for the District of Utah.Online contact led investigators to missing girlThe FBI's Salt Lake City Field Office received information from a family member on August 20, last year, that the girl had disappeared around May 29 that year. Her parents had subsequently filed a missing-person report in June, according to an FBI agent's sworn statement cited by Oregon news outlet KGW8.The FBI's inquiry also examined the girl's online activity. According to the complaint, investigators traced her interactions to gaming platforms, where the initial contact occurred, before the conversations shifted to social media. Her parents had separately informed authorities that she was exchanging sexually explicit images and videos online for money. The family had also raised concerns about her self-harm.The agency reviewed information obtained from social media companies and interviewed people linked to the accounts. Investigators said they confirmed that the girl had shared sexually explicit material with online users.A breakthrough came on Sunday when investigators received information about her possible location. The tip followed contact between the missing girl and another minor who had met someone while playing the online game Among Us on October 15. Their conversations later continued through a social media application.The person using the account identified herself as the missing girl and told the other minor that she had run away but was being held against her will at a man's home in Oregon. She also said police were no longer looking for her and shared news reports about her disappearance, according to the complaint.FBI monitored video call before rescueInvestigators arranged a video call between the girl and a family member on Sunday, with FBI agents monitoring the conversation. During the call, she identified Harmel as a man she had met online around May 2025, according to KGW8.She told investigators that Harmel had offered her money to travel to Oregon and later drove from Oregon to Perry, Utah, to pick her up. The complaint alleges that he threw her phone into a river in Logan Canyon before taking her to his residence.The complaint further alleges that Harmel forced her to remove her braces with pliers to make it harder for authorities to identify her. She also told investigators that he had hit her and sexually assaulted her during her time at the residence. The alleged assaults took place in both 2025 and 2026, according to the complaint.Girl recovered from Huntington residenceOregon State Police said officers responded to a residence on Fulton Street East in Huntington shortly before noon on Sunday, following a request from the FBI to locate the missing teenager. They took her into protective custody and arranged medical treatment and evaluation, according to the federal complaint.A search of the property recovered knives, women's clothing and sexual lubricant. Items initially suspected to be firearms were identified as BB guns, the complaint states.Investigators also interviewed another resident, who said Harmel had travelled to Utah in 2025 to meet the girl before bringing her back to Oregon. The resident described the girl as Harmel's new girlfriend, according to the complaint.Man faces federal chargeHarmel is charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. articles.title: An 80-year-old British Columbia woman left a C$5.5 million estate to charity, but after she died a friend produced photocopies of a will naming herself sole heir; on October 29, a court ruled the charities get it all
articles.summary: An inheritance dispute involving a C$5.5 million estate has ended with a significant victory for charity in British Columbia.
articles.body: An inheritance dispute involving a C$5.5 million estate has ended with a significant victory for charity in British Columbia. When 80-year-old Shirley Isobel Alexander died in April 2025, she left behind a carefully documented estate plan directing her wealth towards charitable causes. But after her death, a woman claiming to be her friend came forward with photocopies of a different will that allegedly named her as the sole beneficiary. The competing claims eventually landed in court, where the Supreme Court of British Columbia delivered its decision on October 29, 2026, ruling in favour of Alexander's original charitable intentions.A fortune intended for charitable causesAlexander, who lived in Lac La Hache, British Columbia, died on April 29, 2025, without a spouse or children. Her estate was valued at approximately C$5.5 million, with her first cousins among her closest relatives.According to Clark Wilson LLP, her estate planning dated back to March 2018, when she signed a will prepared by her lawyer. It directed her wealth towards registered charities and foundations she had identified in writing. It also gave her executor limited discretion to select charitable organisations if necessary.Several years later, Alexander decided to make one important change. The lawyer named as executor in her original will had been disbarred, prompting her to appoint a trust company instead. In April 2025, she met with a new lawyer in Williams Lake and signed a codicil confirming the provisions of her 2018 will while replacing the executor.She also completed a beneficiary designation directing her estate towards a donor-advised fund, accompanied by instructions outlining the charitable causes she wanted to support.The photocopied will that changed everythingThe dispute began after Alexander's death, when a woman described as her friend produced photocopies of documents that appeared to tell a very different story.As detailed by Clark Wilson LLP, the woman presented two versions of a purported will dated November 8, 2024. One named her as Alexander's sole beneficiary and appointed her as co-executor alongside the trust company. The second version had the date and the trust company's appointment crossed out, without initials or a replacement date.She also produced a typed but unsigned letter dated April 15, 2025. According to her account, Alexander had handed her the documents in sealed envelopes with instructions to open them after her death.However, the original documents and envelopes were never produced, and the identities of the alleged witnesses to the 2024 will remained unknown. The woman challenged the validity of the April codicil, questioned Alexander's mental capacity and sought to have the photocopied documents recognised as her final testamentary instructions.Why the court rejected the claimThe Supreme Court examined the competing evidence, including Alexander's personal journals, financial records, legal documents and electronic devices. Two searches of her home uncovered her original 1991 will and a copy of the 2018 document, but nothing connected to the alleged 2024 will or the unsigned letter.Clark Wilson LLP notes that a forensic examination of her devices also found no trace of the disputed documents. Her journals, which recorded much of her daily life, contained no reference to signing a new will or handing over sealed envelopes.The court also considered evidence from her lawyer and financial advisor, who had known her for more than 25 years. The drafting lawyer provided detailed accounts of his meeting with Alexander, including discussions about her assets, family circumstances and charitable intentions.The court found the April 2025 codicil valid and confirmed that it upheld the 2018 will. It also concluded that neither version of the alleged 2024 document met the requirements for probate. The unsigned letter was rejected because it did not demonstrate final testamentary intentions.The C$5.5 million estate goes to charityIn its October 29 decision, Alexander Estate (Re), 2026 BCSC 2092, the court admitted the 2018 will and the 2025 codicil to probate in solemn form, rejecting the competing documents.The ruling also highlighted an important distinction in estate disputes: photocopies alone are not necessarily enough to establish the validity of a will. Under British Columbia's Wills, Estates and Succession Act, courts can sometimes correct deficiencies in testamentary documents, but only when reliable evidence establishes that they are authentic and reflect the deceased's final intentions.As Clark Wilson LLP explains, the case ultimately turned on the strength of the evidence. Detailed records, independent witnesses and a properly documented estate plan proved far more convincing than unverified photocopies and conflicting accounts.For Alexander, the decision means that the charitable legacy she had spent years putting in place will stand, rather than being displaced by documents that the court found insufficient to establish her final wishes.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: A California charity finance manager stole $1.6 million meant for youth education programmes and spent it on a Hawaii condominium and luxury sports tickets
articles.summary: Carrie Lynn Grant, a finance manager at a Northern California charity that provides educational materials and programmes to prepare young people to
articles.body: Carrie Lynn Grant, a finance manager at a Northern California charity that provides educational materials and programmes to prepare young people to succeed in a global economy, has been sentenced to 27 months in federal prison for embezzling more than $1.6 million. According to a press release from the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California, Grant deposited charity money into her personal account and created fraudulent records to cover her tracks between November 2017 and June 2023. The release states that she spent the money on, among other things, first-class air travel, floor seats for a Golden State Warriors game, box seats for a San Francisco 49ers game, and a condominium in Hawaii.What is included in the $465,000 Chicago church property listingThe release states that Grant, 62, of Pleasant Hill, California, was indicted by a federal grand jury on 22 July 2024. It adds that she pleaded guilty on 11 August 2025 to one count of wire fraud.The announcement was made by United States Attorney Craig Missakian and FBI Acting Special Agent in Charge Agustin Lopez. According to the US Attorney's Office, Assistant US Attorney Evan M. Mateer is prosecuting the case with the assistance of Christine Tian and Amala James. The office said the prosecution is the result of an investigation by the FBI.How did the charity finance manager hide the fraudAccording to the plea agreement and court documents, as cited in the press release, Grant committed the offence over a period of years, from November 2017 to June 2023. The release states that she "abused her role as the finance manager of the charity." It says she deposited charity money into her personal account while creating fraudulent records to cover her tracks.The US Attorney's Office said that in total, Grant stole more than $1.6 million from the non-profit organisation. The charity, according to the release, is one that provides educational materials and programmes aimed at preparing young people for a global economy.The press release states that Grant spent the money on, among other things, first-class air travel, floor seats for a Golden State Warriors game, box seats for a San Francisco 49ers game, and a condominium in Hawaii. The office listed these as examples and did not say they were the only purchases.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Houston woman Roda Osman raised more than $42,000 on GoFundMe after claiming a man hit her with a brick, was charged with theft by deception and has since been convicted
articles.summary: Roda Osman, the Houston woman known online as the “Brick Lady”, was convicted of theft by a Harris County jury over a GoFundMe fundraiser that raised
articles.body: Roda Osman, the Houston woman known online as the “Brick Lady”, was convicted of theft by a Harris County jury over a GoFundMe fundraiser that raised $42,302 on her claim that a man hit her in the face with a brick after she refused to give him her phone number. Police charged her with theft by deception in January 2024, and the jury returned its guilty verdict in October 2025 after hearing three days of testimony. She was then sentenced to 10 years of probation, and she and her defence team said in court that they would appeal the conviction.What Osman told officers about the brick, the car and the Uber driverKPRC reported that Houston police officers responded to an aggravated assault call on 3 September 2023 and met Osman and a female friend. Officers noted that Osman was intoxicated, hostile and irate.In her original report at the scene, Osman said she was walking on Schumacher Lane when an unknown man threw a brick at her because she would not give him her phone number, according to court documents. She also said she had ordered an Uber and believed the man who threw the brick was the driver, that she got into his car, and that he then tried to kidnap her. Osman added that the man was involved in human trafficking and had a large group of women in the car.How the story went viral on Instagram and how a GoFundMe page was set up the next dayBusiness Insider reported that in a video later taken down, Osman appeared in a hospital gown with a swollen face. She said a man picked up a brick in front of many other men and asked what they were going to do about it, and she accused those men of doing nothing. Osman also went live on Instagram, and the video linked from her fundraiser received more than one million likes. Online, she became known as the “Brick Lady”, and many creators debated what had happened.A GoFundMe page called “Help Roda Recover”, listing Osman as the beneficiary, was created on 4 September, the day after the reported assault. Its description said she was viciously attacked with a brick by a man whose number she refused to give, and that onlookers stood by and did not even call an ambulance. By 25 October 2023, it had raised $42,302, according to the charging documents.Police alleged in the complaint that Osman had a friend start the page based on the brick story. Several donors reported it as fraudulent, and it was frozen.GoFundMe said in a statement that it has zero tolerance for misuse of its platform and cooperates with law enforcement. The fundraiser has been removed, all donors have been refunded and Osman has been barred from using the site.Why detectives doubted the account: a friend’s doubts, a changed story and surveillance footageOn 15 September, detectives tried to reach Osman but found that the number she had given belonged to her friend. The friend told them she was not from Houston and had gone drinking at several places with Osman, who called male friends to pick them up. She said she heard Osman cry out that she had been hit, but heard no argument beforehand. According to the charging documents, she also said she did not believe Osman had been hit with a brick.A detective finally reached Osman by phone on 19 September. Osman said a dark-coloured sedan pulled up as she left a club, that she assumed it was the Uber she had called, and that the man inside hit her in the face with a brick. She also said she had carried out her own investigation and identified the man. When the detective asked where her friend was, Osman became upset and said she was far away, talking to another man. Osman then changed her account, saying she was instead assaulted at a club. After further questions, she asked for the detective’s supervisor and hung up.On 20 September, detectives canvassed the area and obtained footage from surveillance cameras in the 5600 block of Schumacher Lane. It shows Osman, her friend and the man she named walking into a lounge together. About 20 minutes later, the three came out and, with an unidentified driver, got into a white Maserati. Osman and the man argued in the back seat, according to the charging documents. When they got out, the detective’s affidavit says Osman hit the man in the face with an unknown object, and he struck her in the face with a plastic water bottle in response. Detectives described Osman as the aggressor and said the footage did not match her recorded statement.A 2020 fundraiser in Minneapolis with a similar claim, and what Minneapolis police told detectivesWhile the investigation was under way, a mental health advocate and TikTok blogger called detectives because she believed Osman was running a scam, citing a similar situation in Minneapolis in 2020. She pointed them to a 2020 GoFundMe page created by or for Osman. It had a $5,000 goal to cover medical bills, legal fees and a new phone after a claimed attack by private security that left facial bruising, a black eye and leg injuries.Minneapolis police told Houston police they had no record of any report that Osman was assaulted in 2020. Osman’s former roommate, who was living with her when the first fundraiser was created, also contacted detectives. She said she ended the friendship after finding out Osman was scamming people, and that the donation request was based on a false story.The theft by deception charge, a $50,000 bail request and a planned surrender that never happenedThe Harris County District Attorney’s Office asked the court to set bail at $50,000 on the theft charge. Osman was already on bail for a separate offence dated 22 September 2023, which court records list as felony assault and domestic violence.She had agreed to surrender at a quarter to four in the afternoon on Thursday 18 January 2024, but did not arrive. Community activists Candence Matthews and Quannel X said Osman had contacted them for help and that they had arranged the surrender with her. They said it was the first time someone they had worked with failed to show up.She says she was assaulted, police are lying, and a friend made the fundraiserOsman told Business Insider in January 2024, when she was 33, that on the night in question she and her friend met two men while going clubbing, and that one of them pestered her for her phone number all night even though she turned him down. She said that at around four or five in the morning, as the group stood on the street deciding whether to call an Uber, the man forced her to touch him sexually and choked her. When she tried to get away, she said, he hit her over the head with something and ran to his friend’s car. She then saw a brick on the ground and assumed he had used it. The affidavit does not mention her claim that he forced her to touch him.She said police were lying about the surveillance footage, that she never held an object, and that what hit her could have been a liquor bottle. She called police afterwards and was taken to hospital by ambulance. Hospital records she shared with the outlet show a doctor reported a bruise on the left side of her face and blood coming from her left ear. She said she could not recall everything clearly because she had been hit on the head, had a concussion and had been drinking. “Not remembering every single detail of assault and trauma is not a crime,” she said.Osman believed police filed the charges in retaliation for her reporting one of the officers who handled her case. The Houston Police Department declined to comment on that allegation. She also said she should not face a fraud charge because she did not create the GoFundMe page, and that her friend made it because she wanted to help. She rejected the claim that the 2020 fundraiser was fraudulent, saying police were taking it from social media and that being attacked more than once is not a crime or a hoax.The jury’s verdict, what the sentence requires and why an appeal is expectedAs per reports from October 2025 that the jury reached its verdict after about two and a half hours of deliberation, and that Osman had to be told to calm down several times when it was returned. Harris County prosecutor Keith Houston said bank records shown at trial revealed all of the donated money had been spent on trips to Jamaica and New York, at restaurants, at spas and on rideshares. Surveillance video showed Osman hitting Olan Douglas, the man she had accused, before he hit her back. Houston said the leading theory for her facial injury is that she hit her head on the car door frame when she went down beside the open door, though exactly what happened is not fully clear.Judge Dan Simons attached conditions to the probation, 90 days in jail, inpatient substance abuse treatment, full restitution of $42,302 and a ban on using social media for 10 years. If she violates the terms, she could serve a 10-year prison sentence. Osman was taken into custody at the end of the trial to begin the 90 days. A $50,000 appeal bond was denied the following morning for unclear reasons, and the appeals process could take more than a year.Douglas also said that Osman made a couple of months of his life “a living hell”, and that he was happy with the verdict and the sentencing plan. In January 2024, he had said he received death threats over the false brick claim.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Wyoming landowner had 640 acres with no legally usable road to reach them; after a neighbouring ranch resisted access, the state’s highest court approved a private road but upheld $61,200 in compensation
articles.summary: A 640-acre property is of little practical use if its owner cannot legally reach it by vehicle.
articles.body: A 640-acre property is of little practical use if its owner cannot legally reach it by vehicle. That problem became the centre of a dispute between two Wyoming landowners after Wagonhound Land & Livestock Company sought access to an isolated parcel surrounded almost entirely by a neighbouring ranch. After negotiations failed, the company approached the court to establish a private road across the neighbouring property, but the ranch challenged the move and disputed the compensation.In its September 23, 2026, decision in Wagonhound Land & Livestock Company, LLC v. Little Medicine Creek Ranch, Inc., available on Justia, the Wyoming Supreme Court upheld the creation of the private road and the $61,200 compensation awarded to the neighbouring ranch. However, it overturned two restrictions imposed on the road, finding that they lacked sufficient supporting evidence.The dispute over access to 640 acresThe dispute concerned Parcel 1, a roughly 640-acre tract in a remote and rugged part of northern Albany County, Wyoming. The property belonged to Wagonhound and was surrounded almost entirely by land owned by Little Medicine Creek Ranch, formerly known as Burnett Ranch.On April 21, 2023, Wagonhound sent the ranch a letter expressing interest in purchasing legally enforceable access to the isolated property. It proposed a 30-foot-wide right-of-way along existing ranch roads and indicated that it was willing to negotiate a fair price. However, the discussions failed to produce an agreement. Wagonhound subsequently filed a petition under Wyoming's private road statute, seeking permission to establish access across the neighbouring ranch.Little Medicine Creek Ranch opposed the request, arguing that Wagonhound already had an outlet through adjoining Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land and could use an alternative route to reach a public road.Why the property was considered landlockedThe ranch argued that an existing two-track route across BLM land provided Wagonhound with access. However, the route eventually crossed state trust land and required passage through approximately 1,700 feet of the neighbouring ranch's private property. The Wyoming Supreme Court found that the existence of a rough track across public land did not, by itself, establish legally enforceable access to a public road. There was no evidence that the general public had used the route, and access to it was effectively controlled by the surrounding private property.The ranch also proposed the Parsons Creek Route, suggesting Wagonhound could obtain permission to construct a bypass across public land. However, that road did not physically exist. BLM employees also questioned whether the proposed route was accessible, while witnesses described parts of it as little more than a trail. The court concluded that neither option provided legally enforceable vehicle access to a public road. It therefore agreed that Wagonhound had established the necessity for a private road.The $61,200 compensation awardThe district court appointed three independent viewers and appraisers to examine possible routes and assess the impact on the neighbouring property. They recommended Wagonhound's proposed route because it was shorter, more direct and more practical than the alternative suggested by the ranch. The alternative would require construction across a rocky ridge and could make winter access difficult.The viewers estimated that the private road would affect 680 acres of the neighbouring ranch. Using comparable property sales and an earlier appraisal report, they calculated a reduction in value of $90 per acre. This resulted in a total compensation award of $61,200, which the district court approved. Little Medicine Creek Ranch challenged the calculation, arguing that the assessment did not account for potential operational losses, including livestock health problems linked to dust, additional staffing expenses and reduced hunting opportunities.However, the Supreme Court upheld the award. It explained that Wyoming's private road statute requires a before-and-after appraisal to determine the reduction in the value of the affected property. It does not provide compensation for indirect future business losses. The court also noted that the ranch had not presented evidence disputing the viewers' calculation of the affected acreage or the $90-per-acre reduction.Changes to the private road conditionsAlthough the court upheld the private road and compensation, it overturned two conditions imposed by the district court. The first required Wagonhound to pay for any damage to the road, regardless of whether its own vehicles, the neighbouring ranch or their guests had caused it. The Supreme Court found no evidence justifying this requirement. Wagonhound remained responsible for maintaining the road for its use, but could not automatically be held liable for damage caused by others.The second restriction prohibited vehicles with more than four axles, including semi-trailers, from using the road. The court found insufficient evidence that heavy vehicles would create unreasonable noise, lighting problems or other disturbances. However, it upheld the requirement that Wagonhound regularly apply water to suppress dust, citing evidence about its potential impact on livestock. The court also rejected the ranch's request to restrict the road exclusively to agricultural use, finding insufficient evidence to justify such a limitation.Final ruling and its implicationsOn September 23, 2026, the Wyoming Supreme Court affirmed the findings on necessity, good faith, route selection and compensation, while reversing parts of two road conditions. The decision allows Wagonhound to obtain legally enforceable vehicle access to its 640-acre property while requiring it to pay the neighbouring ranch $61,200. It also clarifies that a landowner cannot be denied access simply because a rough track crosses public land when no legally usable connection to a public road exists.The ruling was therefore partly in favour of both parties: Wagonhound secured the private road, while Little Medicine Creek Ranch retained its compensation and dust-control protections.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kai Cenat faces fresh controversy as Reggie claims judge issued 12-month stay-away order against him
articles.summary: YouTuber Reginald “Reggie,” known online as “Lil Rodney Son,” says a judge has ordered him to stay away from Kai Cenat for 12 months.
articles.body: YouTuber Reginald “Reggie,” known online as “Lil Rodney Son,” says a judge has ordered him to stay away from Kai Cenat for 12 months. Reggie shared the update after a court appearance on November 3, 2026, and later said Kai had never sued him. His comments add a new turn to their public dispute, which began after Reggie made allegations involving Cenat and Twitch streamer RaKai. Kai had threatened legal action in September, but the court order Reggie described should not be confused with a confirmed lawsuit filed publicly.Reggie says court ordered him to stay away from Kai Cenat for 12 monthsReggie shared his update through Instagram Stories on November 3. He thanked his lawyer and said he was surprised that his song was played in court. He then described the decision:“Why they play my song in court lol they almost had me haha shoutout my lawyer ! The court ruled that I have to stay away from that guy for 12 months that's all nun more nun less.”However, the exact 12-month period has not been confirmed through a public court record or a statement from Kai's side. The Times of India reported on November 4 that other accounts described Kai as receiving a stalking protective order. The reported restrictions also included staying away from AMP properties and not speaking about Kai directly or indirectly. The exact terms have not been verified through a public court document.The dispute started after Reggie made allegations involving Kai and RaKai. Kai responded during a September 30 livestream, rejected the claims and said he planned to take legal action. He also challenged Reggie to contact the police and share any evidence.“I am calling the cops! Yeah! I'm suing you, brother! Like, I'm suing you, bro! And I still have sympathy for you because I know you're not yourself, bro. But it's going too far! You're playing with my name. You're playing with my family's food. You're playing with my future kids' food. That's how deep it goes.”Kai's words showed that he intended to sue, but they did not confirm that a lawsuit had been filed. His legal team later sent Reggie a cease-and-desist letter. Dexerto reported on October 27 that the letter, sent on October 2, demanded that Reggie remove videos containing statements Kai's lawyers called false and misleading. Such a letter is a legal demand, not a court judgment.Reggie says Kai Cenat never sued him and calls court appearance “amazing”During his November 3 TikTok livestream, Reggie disputed the claim that Kai had sued him. He said the court matter was different from what people were saying and repeated that he had been ordered to stay away from Kai.“‘You're getting sued, not prosecuted.’ I was never getting sued. That was the 48. He can't even sue me. See how that works? The judge ruled I gotta stay away from that guy for 12 months. I don't have no intention of going around him. I don't want to harm that guy. I don't want to do nothing to that guy. I don't want to do nothing to nobody. I am a *****. I just rap.”Reggie also praised his lawyer and said he was happy with how the court appearance went. He called himself a “free man” and joked about buying a chain the next day.“The court was amazing, bro. Shout out to my lawyer. Hey, the court was amazing. My lawyer is a beast. Feel me? Shout out to my lawyer. I'm a free man. I'm finna buy a chain. I'm finna buy a chain tomorrow.”As of November 5, Kai had not publicly responded to Reggie's latest comments. The full terms of the court order have not been made public in the reports reviewed, so the 12-month restriction remains based on Reggie's account.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy loses after ugly campaign
articles.summary: Even as Indian-American Democrats enjoyed several victories, the Republican side told a rather different story.
articles.body: Even as Indian-American Democrats enjoyed several victories, the Republican side told a rather different story. Vivek Ramaswamy, entrepreneur and former presidential hopeful who enjoyed Donald Trump's endorsement and considerable attention from the Republican establishment, lost the Ohio gubernatorial contest to Democrat Amy Acton after an ugly campaign which was widely criticised.In Arizona, Democrat Amish Shah was enjoying a promising election night, leading former NFL kicker Jay Feely in the contest for the state's 1st Congressional District, which includes most of Phoenix and Scottsdale. With 54.9% against Feely's 43.2% in the early returns, Shah appeared well positioned to become another Indian-American addition to Congress. The established Indian-American Dem contingent had plenty to celebrate. Ami Bera won an eighth term in California, while Ro Khanna retained his Silicon Valley seat and Pramila Jayapal secured a sixth term in Washington state. Suhas Subramanyam also held Virginia's 10th Congressional District outside Washington DC, consolidating the desi presence in House.Meanwhile, Los Angeles offered perhaps the most intriguing unfinished chapter of the Indian-American electoral story. Nithya Raman, the Kerala-born urban planner and Los Angeles City Council member of a socialist democrat persuasion, was locked in a dead heat with establishment Democrat Karen Bass, with leads changing frequently.There were victories beyond Capitol Hill, too. Maryland's Aruna Miller retained her lieutenant-governorship alongside Governor Wes Moore; Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul won another term; and Aparna Raj won Washington DC Council's Ward 1, which includes some of the most storied areas in capital, including Adams Morgan, Kalorama and Columbia Heights.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2014, a buyer paid $4.7 million for an 1840s Nantucket mansion and restored its original brick floor and hidden well; 12 years later, the 6,106-square-foot historic home sold for $15.25 million on October 27
articles.summary: A historic mansion on Nantucket's Main Street has changed hands for $15.25 million, more than tripling the price it fetched in 2014.
articles.body: A historic mansion on Nantucket's Main Street has changed hands for $15.25 million, more than tripling the price it fetched in 2014. The Greek Revival-style residence, known as the Hadwen-Wright House or the Two Greeks, dates back to the 1840s and is among the island's most distinctive examples of historic residential architecture. The sale was reported by Mansion Global and the Nantucket Current, while local publication Nantucket Current and property records provide further details about the home's history and ownership. The 6,106-square-foot property was sold on October 27, 2026, after being listed for $15.5 million in August.A mansion built during Nantucket's whaling eraKnown as the Hadwen-Wright House, the property at 94 Main Street was designed by local architect and builder Frederick Brown Coleman for wealthy whale-oil merchant William Hadwen. It was completed in 1847, during a period when Nantucket's whaling industry was beginning to decline.The mansion is part of a pair of neighbouring Greek Revival residences known as the Two Greeks. Its identical-looking neighbour at 96 Main Street was built first for Hadwen himself, while the more elaborately decorated 94 Main Street was constructed for his niece. According to the Town of Nantucket's historic records, the two buildings represent the Greek Revival style at its height, with imposing columns, temple-like entrances and prominent porticos. The Hadwen-Wright House is particularly distinguished by its four Corinthian columns and carefully preserved architectural details.Restoration work uncovered a hidden piece of historyThe previous owner purchased the property in October 2014 for $4.7 million from the estate of Katherine Lodge, a local preservationist who had been its longtime steward. During her ownership, she undertook several renovation and restoration projects while retaining the building's historic character. The work included updating its mechanical systems and renovating the kitchen, alongside carefully restoring original features.One particularly detailed project involved the basement's original brick flooring. Rather than replacing it, the owner had each brick removed, numbered and documented before installing a new subfloor and moisture barrier. The original bricks were then returned to their respective positions. Another discovery came during the restoration when workers found a large slate stone covering a deep, brick-lined cistern that still contained water. Instead of removing it, the owner chose to preserve the structure. It can now be viewed through a glass-covered opening illuminated from within, allowing visitors to look down into the historic well. The restoration also retained original woodwork, fireplaces, wide-plank pine floors and the mansion's distinctive staircase.Two domes, five bedrooms and a view of NantucketSpread across four levels, the 6,106-square-foot residence combines historic architecture with modern amenities. It has five bedrooms, six full bathrooms and an additional half-bathroom, along with several formal sitting and entertaining spaces.Two domes are among its most distinctive features. The larger one sits above the primary bedroom suite, while the smaller dome crowns a rounded nook near the top of the wooden staircase. The property also features a belvedere offering views across Nantucket's historic district towards the harbour. Outside, the grounds include a paved terrace, landscaped garden, trees and space for growing vegetables. Much of the interior remains protected under a historic preservation easement, helping ensure that the architectural character of the original building is maintained.The historic property sells for $15.25 millionThe mansion was listed for $15.5 million on August 5, 2026, through Maury People Sotheby's International Realty. It reportedly went under agreement shortly after being listed, before officially changing hands on October 27 for $15.25 million.According to Nantucket Current, the property was purchased by John E. Kozlowski, trustee of the 94 Main Street Nominee Trust, from Nomor LLC. The latest transaction represents an increase of $10.55 million over its 2014 purchase price, reflecting the property's continued appeal as both a historic residence and a significant piece of Nantucket's architectural heritage.The sale brings renewed attention to a home that has survived nearly two centuries of change on the island. While its ownership has changed, much of the craftsmanship that made it distinctive in the 1840s remains intact, including architectural details and even a hidden water cistern preserved beneath its floors.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Faridabad man invests Rs 3 crore to open a gym, earns Rs 20 lakh in monthly sales but saves only Rs 2-3 lakh after expenses and EMI
articles.summary: A gym filled with equipment, hundreds of members and monthly sales of Rs 20 lakh may look like a highly profitable business.
articles.body: A gym filled with equipment, hundreds of members and monthly sales of Rs 20 lakh may look like a highly profitable business. But behind the mirrors, machines and membership counters are expenses that can take away a large share of the revenue.Nitesh Yadav, a gym owner from Faridabad, Haryana, recently offered a glimpse into these numbers through an Instagram video titled “How much I earn as a gym owner in a month”. He explained that although his fitness centre records around Rs 20 lakh in monthly sales, the money left after operating costs and loan repayments is considerably smaller.According to Yadav, he invested around Rs 3 crore to establish the gym. He estimates that after paying staff, rent, electricity, other expenses and a monthly loan instalment, he is left with savings of roughly Rs 2 lakh to Rs 3 lakh. His account offers a reminder that high business revenue does not necessarily translate into equally high personal earnings.Rs 20 lakh in sales, but where does the money go?Running a large fitness centre involves more than buying exercise machines and attracting members. Salaries, rent, electricity and regular maintenance create substantial monthly costs. Yadav said staff salaries alone account for around Rs 6 lakh to Rs 7 lakh every month. The gym's rent is another major expense. He initially described the monthly amount, including GST, as approximately Rs 4 lakh. In a reply to a social media user, he later shared the exact rent as Rs 3,39,000, plus 18% GST.Electricity adds another Rs 70,000 to Rs 1 lakh to the monthly bill. Miscellaneous expenses, he said, can range between Rs 1 lakh and Rs 3 lakh. Based on his estimates, these operating expenses leave around Rs 5 lakh to Rs 6 lakh in the scenario he described. However, this is not the amount he can simply take home. The business also has to meet its loan repayments and other financial commitments. His explanation highlights the difference between sales, operating surplus and actual savings. A business may collect a considerable amount from customers every month, but much of that money is already committed to keeping the doors open.The Rs 3 crore investment comes with a monthly EMIThe gym's initial investment was around Rs 3 crore, according to Yadav. He clarified that this amount covered more than just fitness equipment. It included interiors, three months of advance rent, three months of maintenance and marketing expenses. That investment also means a significant loan repayment. Yadav said the monthly EMI is around Rs 3 lakh. Once this amount is deducted from the estimated Rs 5 lakh to Rs 6 lakh remaining after operating expenses, his savings fall to approximately Rs 2 lakh to Rs 3 lakh. Personal and household expenses further influence how much money is ultimately available to him.Yadav also pointed out that a premium gym cannot remain competitive without continued investment. Equipment needs attention, facilities must be maintained, and customer expectations keep changing. The money spent on setting up a gym is therefore not necessarily the last major expense its owner will face. He summed up the reality by saying that business owners must keep up with the market and that appearances can be misleading. A successful-looking establishment does not mean every rupee coming in becomes profit.700 active members paying Rs 6,000 eachAfter the video attracted attention, social media users began asking about the gym's membership numbers and fees. Responding to one question, Yadav said the fitness centre has around 700 active members and charges Rs 6,000 for a monthly membership. This gives an idea of the customer base supporting the business, although membership revenue can vary with renewals, payment cycles and the type of membership purchased. Users also wanted to know what the Rs 3 crore investment covered. Yadav clarified that it included equipment, interiors, advance rent, maintenance and marketing, rather than the gym building itself.The discussion also brought comparisons with smaller neighbourhood gyms. One user argued that local gym owners may earn better margins because they can start with an investment of Rs 50 lakh or less and operate with fewer employees. The user suggested that a smaller setup with a maximum of three staff members could leave more money after expenses and EMIs. Another commenter questioned whether gyms were suitable businesses for people primarily seeking high profits, given the substantial fixed investment involved. Yadav agreed that the business could be difficult financially unless sales were exceptionally strong.Why retaining members matters more than new sign-upsYadav's video also drew attention to a key part of running a gym: keeping existing members. In the caption accompanying his post, he described gym income as membership revenue minus rent, staff salaries and maintenance. He added that real profit comes from member retention, rather than simply bringing in new customers.The point is important because a gym's monthly sales depend on people continuing to use and renew their memberships. If members leave, the business must keep attracting new customers to maintain its revenue. At the same time, fixed expenses such as rent, salaries and electricity continue even when membership numbers fluctuate.Yadav's account is a personal disclosure, not an independently audited financial statement. His figures illustrate the costs of running his particular premium gym and should not be treated as a standard profit estimate for every fitness centre. Still, his experience challenges the assumption that a business generating Rs 20 lakh in monthly sales automatically makes its owner wealthy. In a capital-intensive business, the size of the investment, the cost of operations and the ability to retain customers can matter just as much as revenue.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who is Hakeem Jeffries? Democratic leader poised to become first Black US House speaker
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries is set to become the first Black Speaker of the US House of Representatives, marking a historic moment in American politics after the Democrats gained control in the 2026 midterm elections. Learn more about Jeffries' background, political priorities, and what this milestone means for the future of the US Congress.
articles.body: Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats secured majority control of the chamber in the 2026 midterm elections, setting up a historic change in congressional leadership. The 56-year-old New York lawmaker is expected to be formally elected when the new Congress convenes on January 3.Jeffries' elevation would mark a milestone in the history of the US Congress, more than 150 years after Joseph Rainey became the first Black American elected to the House in 1870. The speakership is the only congressional leadership position established by the US Constitution and places its holder second in the presidential line of succession.Addressing supporters at a Democratic election watch party in Washington, Jeffries was greeted with chants of "Speaker! Speaker!" as his party celebrated its return to the House majority."This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one," Jeffries said, adding that voters had called for significant political change."We hear you," he said. "We're going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve."Jeffries has led House Democrats for four years and is expected to succeed Republican Mike Johnson. His rise would also make him the highest-ranking Black elected official in the country.Who is Hakeem Jeffries?Born in Brooklyn, New York, Jeffries grew up in a family with an Air Force veteran father and a social worker mother. He has said that witnessing the effects of the crack epidemic in his neighbourhood influenced his decision to enter public service.In an interview with The Associated Press during the campaign, Jeffries said his upbringing gave him a desire to improve conditions for working people who remained in their communities despite difficult circumstances.He studied at the State University of New York at Binghamton, earned a master's degree in public policy from Georgetown University and graduated magna cum laude from New York University School of Law.Before entering Congress, Jeffries worked as a corporate lawyer and served in the New York State Assembly, according to the news agency. He first ran for public office at 29 and lost two campaigns for state government before challenging a 30-year congressional incumbent in 2012. The incumbent stepped aside, allowing Jeffries to win the seat.He represents parts of Brooklyn that were previously represented by Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman elected to Congress. Jeffries is also a member of the Congressional Black Caucus.Known for incorporating references to old-school hip-hop into his speeches, Jeffries has developed a public profile that combines his political messaging with his Brooklyn background. He is married and has two children.Challenges ahead as Democrats take control of the HouseJeffries will lead a Democratic majority facing pressure to deliver on economic concerns while scrutinising President Donald Trump's administration. In a letter to fellow Democrats on Wednesday, he outlined three priorities for the next Congress: affordability, accountability and American values.He has also promised a 100-day agenda focused on reducing living costs and launching congressional investigations into the administration. Impeachment remains among the options under consideration.Jeffries is expected to work alongside Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, who is in line to become majority leader, and Representative Pete Aguilar of California, who is expected to serve as majority whip. The three have led the party together since Jeffries took over from Nancy Pelosi after Democrats lost control of the House in 2022.His election as speaker would also carry historical significance. The US Capitol was built partly by enslaved African Americans, while Joseph Rainey became the first Black member of the House in 1870 during the Reconstruction era. Although Rainey never held the speakership, he was the first Black lawmaker to preside over the House chamber.More than a century and a half later, Jeffries is poised to take control of the speaker's gavel as Democrats prepare to challenge the Trump administration and establish their legislative priorities.You use AI every day.
