articles.title: World record 51 red cards shown in Brazilian youth game
articles.summary: A world record of 43 players and eight members of staff were sent off during an under-20 championship match between Uberlandia and Mamore in Brazil.
articles.body:
A world record of 51 red cards were shown during a chaotic under-20s game in Brazil.

The semi-final first leg of the Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship tie between Uberlandia and Mamore was marred by scenes that led to 43 players and eight members of coaching staff being sent off.

The previous record was 36, in a 2011 fifth-division game between Club Atletico Claypole and Victoriano Arenas in Argentina.

Brazilian news outlet O Tempo reported the military police were called because of extensive damage to the Parque do Sabia Stadium.

According to the referee's report, a brawl broke out in the second half after Mamores' Davi taunted the opposition bench during celebrations when his side went 3-1 up.

Uberlandia goalkeeping coach Paulo Sergio Dias Dos Santos ran on to the pitch to confront him, sparking clashes and the subsequent dismissals, with three players having already been sent off earlier.

The police report referenced 14 broken doors, damaged shower facilities, broken windows and that benches, tables and chairs had been destroyed.

The game was paused for approximately 40 minutes and then abandoned by referee Fernando Patrick Drosghic Modesto.

Uberlandia have since confirmed that they have conceded the second leg of the semi-final because Mamore only have seven players available as a result of all the red cards.

They described their move as a "gesture of fair play" as Mamore would progress through to the final, and Uberlandia will instead focus on the third-place match.

articles.title: Author Michael Morpurgo's charity has taken more than 104,500 children to working farms since 1976; it is marking 50 years by expanding outdoor learning opportunities
articles.summary: Michael Morpurgo and his wife Clare are celebrating 50 years of Farms for City Children, the charity they founded to give young people the chance to
articles.body: Michael Morpurgo and his wife Clare are celebrating 50 years of Farms for City Children, the charity they founded to give young people the chance to experience life on a working farm. Since welcoming its first school in Devon in 1976, the organisation has taken more than 104,500 children and young people into the countryside, where they can care for animals, grow food and learn about nature. As it reaches the milestone in 2026, the charity is looking to build on its work by making outdoor learning and meaningful experiences in nature accessible to more children.Michael Morpurgo’s charity has taken more than 104,500 children to working farmsThe idea behind Farms for City Children began with a belief that children should have opportunities to understand the natural world through direct experience. According to the charity’s website, Michael and Clare Morpurgo established the organisation in 1976, welcoming their first visiting school to Nethercott House in Devon.The couple wanted children, particularly those growing up in urban areas, to experience a different environment from their everyday surroundings. Rather than simply learning about farming from books or lessons, visiting pupils could spend time on a working farm, take part in practical activities and discover how food and nature are connected.The charity's anniversary timeline also highlights the involvement of poet Ted Hughes, who became its founding president in 1976. Over the following decades, the organisation expanded beyond its original Devon base. Lower Treginnis in Pembrokeshire joined the charity in 1989, followed by Wick Court in Gloucestershire in 1998.What do children learn during a week on the farmThe programme is designed to make learning part of everyday farm life. According to the charity’s 2024-25 impact report, visiting children usually spend 5 days at one of its three farms, taking part in activities that connect classroom subjects with practical experience.Their responsibilities include feeding and caring for livestock, planting seeds, harvesting produce and helping prepare meals. They also take part in nature walks, outdoor activities and other tasks that introduce them to the work involved in running a farm.The impact report recorded 3,553 children and young people visiting the farms in the 2024-25 academic year. They represented 116 schools and groups and 482 adults. Thirty-seven per cent of the children and young people involved were eligible for pupil premium funding, and 48% of the school beneficiaries were from the 30% most deprived areas in England and Wales.The report also found improvements in children’s comprehension and confidence. Some 76% said they had a better knowledge of where their food came from, while 72% said they had a better attitude toward perseverance. All school and group leaders surveyed reported a good or outstanding impact of the residential experience on the development of a growth mindset amongst the young people.Importance of outdoor learning beyond the classroomThe charity’s work has become even more important as opportunities for children to get outdoors have become harder to come by. Research cited in an impact report for 2024-25 said nearly half of primary schools in England had cut spending on school trips and enrichment activities due to the cost-of-living crisis.The report also notes that 60% of households experiencing financial strain said they struggled to afford school trips. Meanwhile, 35% of the schools surveyed in research cited by the charity said their pupils would not experience any outdoor learning.Farms for City Children aims to fill this gap by providing residential experiences for children of all backgrounds to explore a different environment. The impact report said all school and group leaders surveyed felt the visits had a good or outstanding effect on children's social connections and wellbeing.The findings also highlighted the environmental benefits of the programme. All surveyed leaders reported a positive impact on young people's awareness of nature, while 99% said the visits improved their understanding of how food travels from farms to consumers.Theresa Moses, headteacher at Paxton Academy, described the school's visit to Wick Court and explained how children who initially appeared hesitant became more curious and confident through practical activities.In her account, published in the charity's article, Moses explained that caring for animals and completing meaningful tasks gave pupils opportunities to succeed outside the familiar classroom environment. She also highlighted how teamwork, resilience and a sense of belonging could develop through shared experiences.She said the effects often continued after children returned home, influencing their conversations, writing, attitudes and confidence.How is the charity marking its golden anniversaryThe 50th anniversary celebrations are also an opportunity to recognise the people who have helped sustain the organisation over five decades. In its January 2026 announcement, Farms for City Children said it would mark the milestone with events across all 3 farms, stories from former visitors and staff, and activities involving schools and community groups.One of the planned activities is an anniversary competition called The further adventures of the Golden Goose, aimed at schools and community groups visiting the farms during 2026.Its anniversary timeline records other important developments in its history. In 1995, the organisation adopted the Goose Girl illustration by Quentin Blake as its logo, following its appearance in Morpurgo's book Muck and Magic. In 2022, it welcomed its first youth community groups during school holidays and began an agroforestry project with the Woodland Trust at Nethercott House.The organisation has also continued developing its educational activities and environmental work. Its 2024-25 impact report describes efforts to create new wildlife habitats, increase biodiversity and introduce more sustainable farming practices across its sites.You use AI every day. articles.title: TFR down, need relook at popn control laws like 2-child norm for polls: SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Observing that laws aimed at controlling population growth in the country had lost their significance because of a fall in the total fertility
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Observing that laws aimed at controlling population growth in the country had lost their significance because of a fall in the total fertility rate (TFR) from 3 to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1, Supreme Court Wednesday said the foundation of such laws had "crumbled", they had become "counter-productive" and their validity, which was upheld by it two decades ago, needed to be re-examined in the present situation.The court then decided to review its 2003 verdict for disqualifying individuals with more than two children from contesting elections to panchayati raj institutions.A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said the earlier perception that population had a negative impact on development did not hold anymore, and not keeping the law abreast of changing times would have consequences far beyond the specific precedent or the law in question."Even though India's population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost significance. If we fail to take note of such demographic changes, India will face serious consequences...," it said. Disqualification provisions on the basis of more than two children for local body polls have been in effect in various states. The court passed the order while examining the validity of a Maharashtra law which was challenged by a woman sarpanch. The court allowed her to hold the post despite the disqualification provision and referred the issue to a larger bench.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US singer Bob Dylan meets Pope Leo XIV in Vatican City
articles.summary: Pope Leo had previously quoted Dylan's work in the preface of a book warning against nuclear rearmament.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.

Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.

The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.

Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.

The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.

Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.

"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.

The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.

It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.

Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.

The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

articles.title: Zelensky speaks with US envoys ahead of trilateral talks
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday said he spoke with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, ahead of trilateral talks with his country, the U.S. and Russia. Zelensky said the three spoke for 90 minutes in anticipation for the talks slated to be held Nov. 10-11. He said the meeting…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday said he spoke with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, ahead of trilateral talks with his country, the U.S. and Russia.

Zelensky said the three spoke for 90 minutes in anticipation for the talks slated to be held Nov. 10-11. He said the meeting was held in Brussels, Belgium, with teams from the U.S., the European Union, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, NATO, the World Bank “and representatives of the global business community.”

“The meeting focused on postwar recovery,” he wrote on the social platform X . “There will be another meeting in Brussels tomorrow on security guarantees for Ukraine. The negotiations must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible.”

“Ukraine is ready to take the necessary steps,” he continued. “Our proposals are clear, and we have given them to the American side. Air defense is an important priority, and we discussed this as well.”

He said Ukraine was in need of Patriot missile systems to “protect lives from Russian attacks,” and called for work with the U.S. to continue working “on each of the bilateral tracks.”

“Peace has no alternative, and postwar security guarantees must be truly cast-iron,” his post concludes. “We are working to make this happen! Glory to Ukraine!”

Witkoff on Monday announced the talks will be held in Abu Dhabi next week. He said that talks with Zelensky and European partners would focus on Ukraine’s security and postwar reconstruction, as well as “economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction.”

The talks come as Trump pushes to end the Russia-Ukraine war as it approaches its five-year mark since Russia invaded the European country. Zelensky has warned that Russia has sought to launch new strikes that would target Ukraine’s “energy and logistics.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to restart the talks next week “in principle,” his foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters after a meeting with Witkoff last month.

Putin said in televised remarks before the meeting that he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of U.S.-Russia ties as well, and to discuss the Iran war, The Associated Press reported. Ushakov said that “large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation” between the U.S. and Russia were also discussed in detail during the meeting with Witkoff.

articles.title: US gets another Indian-origin mayor as Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles election
articles.summary: Indian-origin city council woman Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent mayor Karen Bass to win the Los Angeles mayoral race, marking a significant electoral
articles.body: Indian-origin city council woman Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent mayor Karen Bass to win the Los Angeles mayoral race, marking a significant electoral victory in the United States' second-most populous city.Raman, who was first elected to the Los Angeles City Council in 2020, entered the mayoral race in February, challenging Bass, whom she had publicly endorsed just weeks earlier. The contest subsequently evolved into a generational and political battle, with the two candidates offering different approaches to public safety, affordable housing and homelessness.Bass received the backing of much of the city's political establishment, including the Los Angeles County Federation of Labor and the county's Democratic Party. Raman, meanwhile, secured support from groups that have gained prominence at City Hall in recent years, including the left-wing Democratic Socialists of America and transportation advocacy group Streets For All.The candidates also adopted contrasting campaign strategies in the final days of the race. Bass focused on older voters, visiting senior centres in West Adams and Northridge, where she danced with elderly residents. Raman, on the other hand, campaigned at bars, nightclubs and college campuses, pitching her call for change at City Hall.Bass, a former member of Congress and the California state legislature, secured just 34 per cent of the vote in the June 2 primary, marking a weak showing for an incumbent. Her approval ratings had remained low following the 2025 Palisades fire, which broke out while she was outside the country on a diplomatic mission.During the campaign, Bass highlighted her administration's record on reducing violent crime, accelerating affordable housing projects and addressing homelessness. Her administration said unsheltered homelessness, referring to people living outdoors and in vehicles, had declined by 11 per cent.Raman, however, criticised Bass's approach, describing her efforts to tackle homelessness as costly and ineffective. Citing a reduction in homeless encampments in her own Hollywood Hills district, she pledged to halve street homelessness across Los Angeles by the summer of 2028 and eliminate it entirely by the end of her first four-year term.Both candidates received substantial financial support from outside political groups following the June primary.Homelessness, public safety and affordable housing remained key issues for voters. A poll conducted by Berkeley IGS and the Los Angeles Times between October 19 and 25 found that around 40 per cent of likely voters considered reducing homeless encampments a top priority for the incoming mayor. About 30 per cent identified public safety and the construction of more affordable housing as major concerns.Addressing supporters at her election night gathering at the Greek Theatre plaza on Tuesday, Raman stopped short of declaring victory and urged the crowd to remain cautious."I'm hopeful. I'm very hopeful," Raman told the cheering supporters. "I'm also really superstitious. So we're all just going to be cool, OK? Very cool."Who is Nithya Raman?Born in Kerala in 1981, Raman moved to the United States when she was six and became a US citizen at the age of 22.She completed her undergraduate studies at Harvard University before earning a master's degree in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).Before entering electoral politics, Raman founded Transparent Chennai, an urban research organisation focused on improving sanitation and civic amenities.After moving to Los Angeles in 2013, she worked with the city's municipal administrative officer, helped establish the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition and served as executive director of Time's Up Entertainment.Her projected lead over Bass marks a significant development in the race to lead Los Angeles, with the final outcome still dependent on the completion of vote counting.You use AI every day. articles.title: World’s 50 best restaurants for 2026 revealed
articles.summary: The 50 announced its annual awards for the best restaurants across the globe, and for anyone interested in fine dining, the awards are akin to the Oscars.
articles.body: The best restaurant in the world this year is Asador Etxebarri, an eatery in Atxondo, Spain, that’s nestled in the Basque region and which has become a revered destination restaurant known for a revelatory grilling technique. That’s according to The 50, which announced its 2026 list of the world’s 50 best restaurants at an awards ceremony Wednesday night in Lima, Peru. In remarks given in Spanish after winning, Chef Bittor Arguinzoniz said the prize was “a real honor,” and he cited as inspiration “our mothers and grandmothers,” who, he said, were accomplished cooks. Coming in at No. 2, according to The 50, was Gaggan, located in Bangkok. Formerly known as 50 Best, the company bestows awards for the best restaurants across the globe. The list is compiled based on the votes of the 50 Best Restaurants Academy, which is comprised of more than 1,100 international restaurant industry experts, representing 28 regions around the world. The panel of experts includes food writers and chefs. In addition to restaurants, The 50 also ranks the top bars, hotels and vineyards in the world. The third best restaurant in the world for 2026 was Alchemist, in Copenhagen, Denmark, which was cited for “extraordinary craftsmanship” and where diners should be “prepared for a meal unlike anywhere else.” Rounding out the top five were Quintonil in Mexico City, Mexico, which placed fourth, and Wing in Hong Kong, at No. 5, cited for taking pride in its Chinese heritage and offering diners the “untold stories of Chinese culinary history.” Quintonil was also named the Best Restaurant in Latin America. For anyone interested in fine dining, the awards are akin to the film industry’s Academy Awards (and included almost as much fanfare). Restaurants are eligible for the top prize only once from The 50. Winners are then entered into a separate “Best of the Best” program. The top American entry on the 2026 list was Atomix in New York City, which placed eleventh. The Korean restaurant was named the Best Restaurant in North America, while Chef Junghyun Park was honored with the Chef’s Choice Award and praised for providing a “window into a culture.” Last year, the ceremony was held in Turin, Italy, where Lima’s Maido won the top prize. The 50 is one of several organizations that rank high-end restaurants. Other groups include Michelin and LaListe. The top 50 The academy says it aims to spotlight not just fine dining but cuisine that’s truly innovative. Last year’s winner Maido, for example, was a Peruvian restaurant run by Mitsuharu ‘Micha’ Tsumura, who is a descendant of Japanese immigrants to Peru and uses Japanese cooking techniques. Four out of the five top restaurants in the ranking last year were in Spanish-speaking countries, but other restaurants honored included Piazza Duomo in Alba, Italy, and Steirereck in Vienna, Austria. This year, the top five included restaurants in Asia, North America and Europe. “For the past 25 years, we’ve celebrated the people and places shaping hospitality,” said Rikki Tidball, who heads up the awards program at The 50, in remarks that kicked off the gala event. 1.
